source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf, pp. 2223–2233 (all eleven pages, including the economic-cost panel, Table 4 and references); Table 1, Table 2 and Figure 2 checked on rendered pages 2224–2225

claims.overstatement: None. 'Caused by alcohol' follows the paper's wording, and the claim frames the figure as a model estimate with no intervals.
claims.note: 487, 377 and 111 thousand match Table 1 (p. 2224, checked on the rendered page); 'no uncertainty intervals' is right, and the claim correctly calls these deaths, not new cases. 'An overlapping team' cannot be checked from this source alone (authors: Rehm, Mathers, Popova, Thavorncharoensap, Teerawattananon, Patra). For comparability with the 2020 figures, the claim could say that this model counted all oesophageal and all liver cancers (not only squamous-cell and hepatocellular) and listed 'other neoplasms' among the alcohol-related categories (anchor 2). It could also say that the chronic-disease fractions came from the 2002 assessment (anchor 3).

anchors.locator: Table 1 (alcohol-attributable deaths in thousands by sex and cause, 2004), Cancer row and footnote
anchors.extracted: Cancer deaths attributed to alcohol in 2004: 377 thousand men, 111 thousand women, 487 thousand in all (rounded to the nearest thousand; 377 + 111 = 488 by rounding); no uncertainty intervals. The bracketed 18.5% (men) and 25.0% (women) are cancer's share of all deaths caused by alcohol, not the share of cancer deaths due to alcohol (footnote).

anchors.locator: Identification of disease categories causally linked to alcohol, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (right column)
anchors.extracted: Cancer categories counted: mouth and oropharynx (C00–C14), oesophagus (C15, all types), colon and rectum (C18–C21, added after the 2007 IARC assessment), liver (C22, all types), breast (C50), and 'other neoplasms' (D00–D48); the cancer total is not broken down by site.

Attributable fractions computed from the prevalence of each drinking category and relative risks against no consumption taken from meta-analyses; for chronic diseases the fractions were taken from the comparative risk assessment for 2002 and applied to WHO's 2004 deaths; counterfactual of no alcohol consumption. A model estimate, not a count.

claims.overstatement: None for this source: the figures are presented as model estimates, 'deaths caused' follows the paper's wording, and no amount or advice from this source appears in the claim.
claims.note: Every Rehm 2009 number in the statement and magnitude matches Table 1 (p. 2224, checked on the rendered page) and p. 2229 (under 60: 5.3%, men 7.9%, women 1.9%). Recomputed: 2482 − 227 = 2255; 2255/58,738 = 3.84%, 1944/31,063 = 6.26%, 311/27,674 = 1.12%; 2255 thousand rounds to 2.3 million: same. Wording points: (1) 'A WHO comparative risk assessment for 2004' is loose. This is a Lancet Series paper by CAMH and WHO authors that applied attributable fractions from the 2002 (chronic disease) and 2000 (injury) assessments to WHO's 2004 deaths (anchor 4). (2) The specific work was funded by CAMH, besides the WHO and Swiss support for the underlying assessments (anchor 7). (3) The paper gives no intervals but says, citing WHO 2002, that the uncertainty of alcohol burden estimates has been quantified as fairly low (anchor 5). (4) The authors themselves read the rise from 3.2% (2000) to 3.8% (2004) as an increase, mainly from more women drinking (anchor 2), which bears on the claim's caution that differences between methods are not a trend. 'More than a quarter' unrecorded, 'middle-class cohorts' and 'controversial' all match pp. 2223 and 2231.

anchors.locator: Table 1 (alcohol-attributable deaths in thousands by sex and cause, 2004)
anchors.extracted: Caused: 2482 (men 2039, women 443): unintentional injuries 666 (556, 110), cardiovascular 545 (466, 80), cancer 487 (377, 111), liver cirrhosis 373 (297, 76), intentional injuries 272 (232, 40), neuropsychiatric 135 (109, 25), low birthweight 3, diabetes 0 (<500). Prevented: cardiovascular −215 (−88, −128), diabetes −12 (−8, −4), total −227 (−96, −132). Net 2255 (1944, 311) of 58,738 deaths (31,063, 27,674): 3.8% (men 6.3%, women 1.1%); CRA 2000 3.2% (5.6%, 0.6%). Rounded to thousands; no intervals.

In 2004, 3.8% of global deaths attributed to alcohol (6.3% men, 1.1% women), net of prevented deaths, which were almost all cardiovascular; most deaths caused were injury, cancer, cardiovascular disease and cirrhosis. Authors read the share as having risen since 2000, mainly from more women drinking. Under age 60: 5.3% (7.9% men, 1.9% women), mainly injuries; most prevented deaths at older ages.

anchors.locator: Global alcohol exposure and associated health › Indicators of alcohol consumption, mortality, and burden of disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (right column)
anchors.extracted: Exposure for 2003 from the WHO Global Status Report 2004 and the WHO information system; recorded consumption from taxation records, industry production and sales and FAO data; unrecorded consumption estimated mainly from expert opinion and general-population surveys; abstention and drinking-volume categories from representative national surveys of the 2000s, survey volumes scaled to per-adult consumption.

Alcohol-attributable fraction = ΣPi(RRi − 1)/[ΣPi(RRi − 1) + 1], with relative risks against no consumption from meta-analyses; fractions for chronic diseases taken from the comparative risk assessment for 2002, for injuries from the 2000 assessment, with drinking patterns used for ischaemic heart disease and injuries; same no-alcohol counterfactual for harms and benefits; applied to 2004 deaths by sex, 7 age groups and 14 WHO subregions.

Limitations: unrecorded consumption, more than 25% of the global total, rests mainly on expert opinion; drinking patterns estimated from nearby countries or expert opinion; relative risks from meta-analyses assumed transferable between countries and derived mainly from middle-class cohorts in developed countries (poverty and malnutrition would bias towards underestimation, other biases the opposite); infectious diseases not included. Authors state the uncertainty has been quantified (WHO 2002) as fairly low compared with other risk factors; no intervals given here.

anchors.locator: Alcohol as a risk factor for disease, 3rd paragraph; Conclusions, 3rd paragraph (p. 2231)
anchors.extracted: Regular low-amount drinking linked to lower incidence of ischaemic cardiovascular outcomes and diabetes; the authors call these benefits controversial and far outweighed by harms, but estimate them to give the net burden. Net cardiovascular benefit expected only where light drinking without heavy occasions is common, and only in older people (p. 2231).

The 2000 and 2002 comparative risk assessments underlying the study were supported by WHO and the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health; the specific work by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto; no conflicts of interest declared.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' modelling checklist, high overall: no uncertainty intervals, no sensitivity analysis, net figures resting on disputed protective relative risks.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial; I agree in particular that the 2000-to-2004 rise is read as a trend despite changed methods and inputs.

missed: Cancer categories behind the 487 thousand cancer deaths (p. 2226, Identification of disease categories, 3rd and 4th paragraphs): all oesophageal (C15) and all liver (C22) cancers, colorectal, breast, mouth and oropharynx, and 'other neoplasms' (D00–D48), with no breakdown by site. The card lists them under outcomes but not as a key finding. That matters because cl_alc_cancer_burden compares this figure with a 2020 model that counted only squamous-cell oesophageal and hepatocellular liver cancer.

Citation slip in the panel (p. 2228, 3rd paragraph): the South Korean study's 5% discount rate is referenced to ref. 45, the Thai study; Table 4 gives the Korean study as ref. 52. No effect on the figures.
